It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|1=最上稲荷}} {{ill|Saijo Inari|ja|最上稲荷|12=draft}} is a Buddhist {{ill|inari shrine|simple}}{{Cite web|date=2021-11-18 |title=Saijo Inari (Saijo Inari-san Myokyoji Temple) {{!|12=draft}} 最上稲荷山妙教寺 |url=https://inari.ne.jp/en/ |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=最上稲荷山妙教寺 {{!}}}} It is considered one of the three major Inari shrines of Japan alongside [[Toyokawa Inari]] and [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], although there is little consensus about the grouping.https://inari.ne.jp/about/ {{Infobox Buddhist temple (Japan) | name = Saijō Inari | image = [[File:Saijo Inari 02.JPG|260px]]
Main Hall (Reikō-den) | caption = | location = {{ill||ja|岡山県}} {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|12=draft}} {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|12=draft}} Takamatsu Inari 712, Okayama Prefecture | coordinates = {{Coord|34|42|32.24|N|133|50|0.28|E|region:JP-33_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | mount = Saijō Inari-san | sect = {{ill|Nichiren sect|ja|Nichiren宗|12=draft}} | honzon = {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦如来|lt_ja=久遠実成本師釈迦牟尼仏|lt=Eternal Original Teacher Shakyamuni Buddha|12=draft}}
{{ill|Inari deity|ja|稲荷神|lt_ja=最上位経王大菩薩|lt=Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu|12=draft}} (Gohonzon for Prayers) | founded = (Trad.) {{ill|Tenpyō-shōhō era|ja|天平勝宝|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|Year 752|ja|752nd year|12=draft}}) | founder = (Trad.) {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|12=draft}} | formal_name = Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji | other_name = Saijō Inari
Takamatsu Inari | cultural_properties = Main Hall and others (Registered Tangible Cultural Property of Japan)
Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completion tier 2]][[Category: ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-04-12|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/2192/1/|accessdate=2014-06-07}} ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. Bengara (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|12=draft}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

{{ill|Inari deity|ja|稲荷神|lt_ja=最上位経王大菩薩|lt=Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu|12=draft}} (Gohonzon for Prayers) | founded = (Trad.) {{ill|Tenpyō-shōhō era|ja|天平勝宝|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|Year 752|ja|752nd year|12=draft}}) | founder = (Trad.) {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|12=draft}} | formal_name = Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji | other_name = Saijō Inari

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completion tier 2]][[Category: ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-04-12|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/2192/1/|accessdate=2014-06-07}} ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. Bengara (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|12=draft}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

{{ill|Inari deity|ja|稲荷神|lt_ja=最上位経王大菩薩|lt=Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu|12=draft}} (Gohonzon for Prayers) | founded = (Trad.) {{ill|Tenpyō-shōhō era|ja|天平勝宝|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|Year 752|ja|752nd year|12=draft}}) | founder = (Trad.) {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|12=draft}} | formal_name = Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji | other_name = Saijō Inari

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completion tier 2]][[Category: ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-04-12|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/2192/1/|accessdate=2014-06-07}} ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|1=最上稲荷}} {{ill|Saijo Inari|ja|最上稲荷|12=draft}} is a Buddhist {{ill|inari shrine|simple}}{{Cite web|date=2021-11-18 |title=Saijo Inari (Saijo Inari-san Myokyoji Temple) {{!|12=draft}} 最上稲荷山妙教寺 |url=https://inari.ne.jp/en/ |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=最上稲荷山妙教寺 {{!}}}} It is considered one of the three major Inari shrines of Japan alongside [[Toyokawa Inari]] and [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], although there is little consensus about the grouping.https://inari.ne.jp/about/ {{Infobox religious building | name = Saijō Inari | image = [[File:Saijo Inari 02.JPG|260px]]
Main Hall (Reikō-den) | caption = | location = {{ill||ja|岡山県}} {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|12=draft}} {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|12=draft}} Takamatsu Inari 712, Okayama Prefecture | coordinates = {{Coord|34|42|32.24|N|133|50|0.28|E|region:JP-33_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | mount = Saijō Inari-san | sect = {{ill|Nichiren sect|ja|Nichiren宗|12=draft}} | honzon = {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦如来|lt_ja=久遠実成本師釈迦牟尼仏|lt=Eternal Original Teacher Shakyamuni Buddha|12=draft}}
{{ill|Inari deity|ja|稲荷神|lt_ja=最上位経王大菩薩|lt=Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu|12=draft}} (Gohonzon for Prayers) | founded = (Trad.) {{ill|Tenpyō-shōhō era|ja|天平勝宝|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|Year 752|ja|752nd year|12=draft}}) | founder = (Trad.) {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|12=draft}} | formal_name = Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji | other_name = Saijō Inari
Takamatsu Inari | cultural_properties = Main Hall and others (Registered Tangible Cultural Property of Japan)
Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completion tier 2]][[Category: ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-04-12|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/2192/1/|accessdate=2014-06-07}} ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. Bengara (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|12=draft}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completion tier 2]][[Category: ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-04-12|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/2192/1/|accessdate=2014-06-07}} ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. Approx. 30 minutes on foot or 5 minutes by taxi. During the first three days of the New Year, a special shuttle bus operated by {{ill|Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|ja|下電観光バス|lt=Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|12=draft}} runs from the station’s north exit to the Inariyama bus stop near the approach to Saijō Inari.A direct bus from Tenmaya Bus Station was suspended from September 1, 2018. In previous years, this route would be canceled during the New Year’s traffic restrictions, and the special bus from Bitchū-Takamatsu Station served as a substitute. === By Car === * Large paid parking lots available (prices vary by season). During the New Year and Setsubun seasons, surrounding roads experience heavy congestion, so check the official Saijō Inari website[http://www.inari.ne.jp/inr.71.00.html Official Saijō Inari Website] under “New Year’s Traffic Restrictions” for detour information. * From the {{ill|Okayama-Sōja Interchange|ja|岡山総社インターチェンジ|lt=Okayama-Sōja IC|12=draft}} on the {{ill|Okayama Expressway|ja|岡山自動車道|lt=Okayama Expressway|12=draft}}, travel east on {{ill|National Route 180 (Japan)|ja|国道180号|lt=National Route 180|12=draft}} toward Okayama, then turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Okayama Prefectural Route 241. About 10 minutes by car. * From the {{ill|Kibi Smart Interchange|ja|吉備サービスエリア|lt=Kibi Smart IC|12=draft}} on the {{ill|Sanyō Expressway|ja|山陽自動車道|lt=Sanyō Expressway|12=draft}}, head west on the Okayama City road Sayan-Karakawa line (side road), go north at the Karakawa-ichiba intersection on Okayama Prefectural Route 61, then south at the Nagano intersection onto Prefectural Route 241. About 15 minutes by car. * From downtown Okayama, take National Route 180 west toward Sōja. At Nakagawa-bashi intersection, head north on Prefectural Route 61, and at Nagano intersection go south on Prefectural Route 241. About 30 minutes by car. * From {{ill|Takahashi City|ja|高梁市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sōja City|ja|総社市|12=draft}}, or {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, take National Route 180 east toward Okayama and turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Prefectural Route 241. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. [[Category:Temples in Kita-ku, Okayama]] [[Category:Inari temples]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Municipal Cultural Properties in Okayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Nichiren-shū temples]] [[Category:Inari shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Okayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Japan]] [[Category:Saijo Inari]] [[Category:Unsorted]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category: Completion tier 2]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:refreshing imported pages]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:return the see also]] [[Category:pages which might possibly be incomplete but are most likely complete]] [[Category:I think I cleared all the incomplete or blank pages earlier]] [[Category:Fix draft categories]] === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengara|ja|弁柄}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|12=draft}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Approx. 30 minutes on foot or 5 minutes by taxi. During the first three days of the New Year, a special shuttle bus operated by {{ill|Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|ja|下電観光バス|lt=Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|12=draft}} runs from the station’s north exit to the Inariyama bus stop near the approach to Saijō Inari.A direct bus from Tenmaya Bus Station was suspended from September 1, 2018. In previous years, this route would be canceled during the New Year’s traffic restrictions, and the special bus from Bitchū-Takamatsu Station served as a substitute. === By Car === * Large paid parking lots available (prices vary by season). During the New Year and Setsubun seasons, surrounding roads experience heavy congestion, so check the official Saijō Inari website[http://www.inari.ne.jp/inr.71.00.html Official Saijō Inari Website] under “New Year’s Traffic Restrictions” for detour information. * From the {{ill|Okayama-Sōja Interchange|ja|岡山総社インターチェンジ|lt=Okayama-Sōja IC|12=draft}} on the {{ill|Okayama Expressway|ja|岡山自動車道|lt=Okayama Expressway|12=draft}}, travel east on {{ill|National Route 180 (Japan)|ja|国道180号|lt=National Route 180|12=draft}} toward Okayama, then turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Okayama Prefectural Route 241. About 10 minutes by car. * From the {{ill|Kibi Smart Interchange|ja|吉備サービスエリア|lt=Kibi Smart IC|12=draft}} on the {{ill|Sanyō Expressway|ja|山陽自動車道|lt=Sanyō Expressway|12=draft}}, head west on the Okayama City road Sayan-Karakawa line (side road), go north at the Karakawa-ichiba intersection on Okayama Prefectural Route 61, then south at the Nagano intersection onto Prefectural Route 241. About 15 minutes by car. * From downtown Okayama, take National Route 180 west toward Sōja. At Nakagawa-bashi intersection, head north on Prefectural Route 61, and at Nagano intersection go south on Prefectural Route 241. About 30 minutes by car. * From {{ill|Takahashi City|ja|高梁市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sōja City|ja|総社市|12=draft}}, or {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, take National Route 180 east toward Okayama and turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Prefectural Route 241. [[Category:Temples in Kita-ku, Okayama]] [[Category:Inari temples]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Municipal Cultural Properties in Okayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Nichiren-shū temples]] [[Category:Inari shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Okayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Japan]] [[Category:Saijo Inari]] [[Category:Unsorted]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category: Completion tier 2]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:refreshing imported pages]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Pages from everybodywiki under right title]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:return the see also]] [[Category:pages which might possibly be incomplete but are most likely complete]] [[Category:I think I cleared all the incomplete or blank pages earlier]] [[Category:Fix draft categories]] === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|12=draft}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure {{ill|Empress Kōken|ja|孝謙天皇|lt=Empress Kōken|12=draft}} of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * {{ill|Year 1985|ja|1985th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * {{ill|Year 2009|ja|2009th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * {{ill|Year 2013|ja|2013rd year|12=draft}} (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * {{ill|Year 2014|ja|2014th year|12=draft}} (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengara|ja|弁柄}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|12=draft}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

During the first three days of the New Year, a special shuttle bus operated by {{ill|Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|ja|下電観光バス|lt=Shimo-Den Kankō Bus|12=draft}} runs from the station’s north exit to the Inariyama bus stop near the approach to Saijō Inari.A direct bus from Tenmaya Bus Station was suspended from September 1, 2018. In previous years, this route would be canceled during the New Year’s traffic restrictions, and the special bus from Bitchū-Takamatsu Station served as a substitute. === By Car === * Large paid parking lots available (prices vary by season). During the New Year and Setsubun seasons, surrounding roads experience heavy congestion, so check the official Saijō Inari website[http://www.inari.ne.jp/inr.71.00.html Official Saijō Inari Website] under “New Year’s Traffic Restrictions” for detour information. * From the {{ill|Okayama-Sōja Interchange|ja|岡山総社インターチェンジ|lt=Okayama-Sōja IC|12=draft}} on the {{ill|Okayama Expressway|ja|岡山自動車道|lt=Okayama Expressway|12=draft}}, travel east on {{ill|National Route 180 (Japan)|ja|国道180号|lt=National Route 180|12=draft}} toward Okayama, then turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Okayama Prefectural Route 241. About 15 minutes by car. * From downtown Okayama, take National Route 180 west toward Sōja. At Nakagawa-bashi intersection, head north on Prefectural Route 61, and at Nagano intersection go south on Prefectural Route 241. About 30 minutes by car. * From {{ill|Takahashi City|ja|高梁市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sōja City|ja|総社市|12=draft}}, or {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, take National Route 180 east toward Okayama and turn north at the Bitchū-Takamatsu intersection onto Prefectural Route 241. Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * {{ill|Year 1950|ja|1950th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|12=draft}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * {{ill|Year 1958|ja|1958th year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * {{ill|Year 1972|ja|1972nd year|12=draft}} (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill||ja|Nichiren宗|lt=Nichiren sect}} temple located in {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区|lt_ja=北区|lt=Kita Ward|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama City|ja|岡山市|lt=Okayama City|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|lt=Okayama Prefecture|12=draft}}. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|12=draft}} of Buddhist origin, where the special {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)|12=draft}} style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a {{ill|Torii|ja|鳥居|12=draft}} and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|12=draft}} and a {{ill|Jingū (Shinto)|ja|神宮|lt=jingū-style|12=draft}} structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|12=draft}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|lt=Fushimi Inari|12=draft}} and {{ill|Toyokawa Inari|ja|豊川稲荷|lt=Toyokawa Inari|12=draft}}, though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and {{ill|Yūtoku Inari Shrine|ja|祐徳稲荷神社|lt=Yūtoku Inari|12=draft}}), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{要出典}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|12=draft}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|12=draft}} {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈|lt=Anti-Buddhist movement|12=draft}}. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=draft}} worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, {{ill|Showa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|12=draft}} 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成21st year |lt=Heisei 21|12=draft}} (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|ja|法華経|lt=Lotus Sutra|12=draft}}. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of {{ill|Dakiniten|ja|荼枳尼天|lt=Dakiniten|12=draft}}, considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, {{ill|Emperor Kanmu|ja|桓武天皇|lt=Emperor Kanmu|12=draft}} also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}}’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長6年|lt=Keichō 6|12=draft}} (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|12=draft}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the {{ill|Tendai sect|ja|天台宗|12=draft}} to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|12=draft}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和54th year |lt=Shōwa 54|12=draft}} (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治14th year |lt=Meiji 14|12=draft}} (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in {{ill|Heisei era|ja|平成18th year |lt=Heisei 18|12=draft}} (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect.
