It was then automatically transferred to everybodywiki and recovered from there. In the future it will be good to import the revisions. Check page history in case this page was moved, since the everybodywiki page may have been under a different title[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 20:10, 11 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|1=最上稲荷}} {{ill|Saijo Inari|ja|最上稲荷|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijo Inari|qq=}} is a Buddhist {{ill|inari shrine|simple|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/inari shrine|qq=}}{{Cite web|date=2021-11-18 |title=Saijo Inari (Saijo Inari-san Myokyoji Temple) {{!|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 最上稲荷山妙教寺 |url=https://inari.ne.jp/en/ |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=最上稲荷山妙教寺 {{!}}}} It is considered one of the three major Inari shrines of Japan alongside [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]] and [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], although there is little consensus about the grouping.https://inari.ne.jp/about/ {{Infobox religious building | name = Saijō Inari | image = [[File:Saijo Inari 02.JPG|260px]]
Main Hall (Reikō-den) | caption = | location = [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|ja]] [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]] [[:en:北區|Kita-ku (Okayama)]] Takamatsu Inari 712, Okayama Prefecture | coordinates = {{Coord|34|42|32.24|N|133|50|0.28|E|region:JP-33_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | mount = Saijō Inari-san | sect = {{ill|Nichiren sect|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren sect|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} | honzon = {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|lt_ja=久遠実成本師釈迦牟尼仏|lt=Eternal Original Teacher Shakyamuni Tathāgata Buddha|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata|qq=}}
[[:en:Inari Ōkami|Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu]] (Gohonzon for Prayers) | founded = (Trad.) [[:en:Tenpyō-shōhō|Tenpyō-shōhō era]] 4 ([[:en:752|Year 752]]) | founder = (Trad.) {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} | formal_name = Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji | other_name = Saijō Inari
Takamatsu Inari | cultural_properties = Main Hall and others (Registered Tangible Cultural Property of Japan)
Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|qq=|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|qq=|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|qq=|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|qq=|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|qq=|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|qq=|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|qq=|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|qq=|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|qq=|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|qq=|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|qq=|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|qq=|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|qq=|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|qq=|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|qq=|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|qq=|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|qq=|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|qq=|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|qq=|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===

Reiō-den (Municipal Cultural Property) | website = http://www.inari.ne.jp/mb/ | website_name = Saijō Inari Myōkyō-ji | map = Japan Okayama }} [[File:saijou_inari01.jpg|thumb|Ō-torii (Grand Torii Gate)]] '''Saijō Inari''' ({{lang|ja|最上稲荷}}, Saijō Inari) is a {{ill|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|lt=Nichiren sect|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ja|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}} temple located in [[:en:北區|Kita Ward]], [[:en:Okayama|Okayama City]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]]. Its formal name is '''Saijō Inari-san Myōkyō-ji'''. Because it is situated in the Takamatsu area of Kita Ward, it is also known as '''Takamatsu Inari''' ({{lang|ja|高松稲荷}}). This temple is renowned as a rare {{ill|Inari shrine|ja|稲荷|lt=Inari|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}} of Buddhist origin, where the special [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism)]] style of worship is permitted. Even though it is a Buddhist temple, it features elements such as a [[:en:Torii|Torii]] and a main hall (Reikō-den) with a {{ill|Shimenawa|ja|しめ縄|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimenawa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 注連縄|1=shimenawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1887421}} and a [[:en:List of Jingū|jingū-style]] structure, preserving many forms from the era of syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism.[https://inari.ne.jp/about/ About Saijō Inari (Japanese)]
It is regarded as one of the '''{{ill|Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|ja|稲荷神#日本三大稲荷|lt=Japan’s Three Great Inari Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Great Inari Shrines of Japan|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}''', along with {{ill|Fushimi Inari Taisha|ja|伏見稲荷神社|1=Fushimi Inari-taisha|lt=Fushimi Inari|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari Taisha|13=User:Immanuelle/Fushimi Inari-taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伏見稲荷大社}} and [[:en:Toyokawa Inari|Toyokawa Inari]], though which three are included varies by tradition.There are various theories about which shrines constitute the Three Great Inari. Fushimi Inari Taisha does not define the other two. Toyokawa Inari’s selection differs (Fushimi and [[:en:Yūtoku Inari Shrine|Yūtoku Inari]]), while Yūtoku Inari Shrine may name Fushimi and Saijō instead.{{Citation needed}} During the first three days ({{ill|Sanganichi|ja|正月三が日|lt=the first three days of New Year|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanganichi|1=Shōgatsu Sanganichi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545488}}) of the New Year, it attracts the largest number of visitors in Okayama Prefecture, over 600,000.[https://www.asahi.com/sp/articles/ASM124HZCM12PPZB00C.html (Asahi Shimbun) New Year’s pilgrims at Saijō Inari, Okayama] == History and Overview == It is said to be the only place in Okayama Prefecture that escaped damage during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治初年|lt=Meiji era|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}} [[:en:Haibutsu kishaku|Anti-Buddhist movement]]. Thus, it still retains a Nichiren-sect style of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]] worship.
Although it is a temple with a long history, it once became independent from the Nichiren sect for a period following World War II (on July 24, [[:en:Shōwa era|Shōwa]] 29 [1954], it became the headquarters of Saijō Inari-kyō Myōkyō-ji), and later returned to the Nichiren sect in July [[:en:2009|Heisei 21]] (2009).
Because this is the birthplace of Saijō-son faith, it is also called the Main Head Temple of Saijō Inari. === Honzon (Principal Deity) === The Gohonzon for prayers is Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu (Inari Daimyōjin). “Saijō-i Kyōō” refers to the [[:en:Lotus Sutra|Lotus Sutra]]. The image is depicted as a celestial maiden (tennyo) riding a white fox, holding a sickle in the right hand and carrying a bundle of rice on the left shoulder, similar to the form of [[:en:Dakini|Dakiniten]], considered the honji (true form) of the Inari deity. === Founding Legend === According to temple tradition, in Tenpyō-shōhō 4 (752), {{ill|Hōon Daishi|ja|報恩大師|lt=Hōon Daishi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōon Daishi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} performed rituals at Hachijō-iwa in the Kibi mountains by imperial order to cure [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] of illness. He had a vision of Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu, and the Empress recovered fully. This is said to be the shrine’s origin. Later, [[:en:Emperor Kanmu|Emperor Kanmu]] also recovered from illness due to prayers by Hōon Daishi. In gratitude, Kanmu offered to build a temple. On the day the master was searching for a spiritual site, Saijō-i Kyōō Daibosatsu told him, “Build your halls at the foot of Ryūōzan in Bitchū Province.” He reported this to the Emperor, who promptly endowed Ryūōzan Jingū-ji as a prayer hall. This became the present Myōkyō-ji. === From Early Modern Period Onwards === Though destroyed by fire during [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]’s invasion of Chūgoku, it was restored in [[:en:Keichō|Keichō 6]] (1601) by {{ill|Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|ja|花房職秀|lt=Hanabusa Shigeyuki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanabusa Tsuneyuki|1=Hanabusa Motohide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615416}}, a hatamoto who governed this area. He invited Nichien Shōnin from the Kantō region and revived it as “Inari-san Myōkyō-ji,” converting from the [[:en:Tiantai|Tendai sect]] to the Nichiren sect. The Reiō-den’s main hall (the old main hall), built in {{ill|Kanpō era|ja|寛保元年|lt=Kanpō 1|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpō era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (1741), is designated as an Important Cultural Property of Okayama City. The current main hall (Reikō-den) was constructed in [[:en:1979|Shōwa 54]] (1979). The original Root Main Hall (Konpon Daidō) built in [[:en:1881|Meiji 14]] (1881) deteriorated and was relocated and restored in [[:en:2006|Heisei 18]] (2006). In 2009, the main hall (Konpon Daidō) and 32 other buildings were registered as Registered Tangible Cultural Properties of Japan. In Shōwa 29 (1954), after the implementation of the Religious Corporations Act (1951), prompted by believers and scholars, the 23rd generation priest Inari Nissen detached from the Nichiren sect and formed the Saijō Inari-kyō religious corporation as a separate sect. However, 55 years later, on July 24, Heisei 21 (2009), the temple and its branch temples returned to the Nichiren sect under the direction of the 26th-generation Inari Nichiō. Although it returned as an ordinary temple of the Nichiren sect, it continues to be referred to as the “Head Temple of Saijō Inari.” During the New Year (Hatsumōde) season, from January 1 to 15, the “New Year’s Good Fortune Grand Prayer Festival” is held, drawing about 600,000 visitors, making it the most visited place in Okayama Prefecture during that period. === Timeline === * [[:en:1950|Year 1950]] (Shōwa 25): A forest fire broke out this year, destroying the {{ill|Niōmon|ja|仁王門|lt=Niō Gate|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Niōmon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金剛力士|1=Nio|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q539715}}.{{Cite news|title=Renovation of Saijō Inari’s Niōmon completed, ceremony held|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2013-12-03|url=http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205083602/http://www.sanyo.oni.co.jp/news_s/news/d/2013120311535272/|archivedate=2013-12-05|accessdate=2014-06-07}} * [[:en:1958|Year 1958]] (Shōwa 33): The Niō Gate was rebuilt, and golden Niō statues and white fox statues were placed inside. * [[:en:1972|Year 1972]] (Shōwa 47): A grand torii (Ō-torii) was erected in the Takamatsu area of Okayama CityTakamatsu was the name of this area in Kita Ward, Okayama City at that time.. The torii is 27.5m tall, with pillars 4.6m in diameter, weighing 2,800 tons.{{Cite news |title=Saijō Inari’s grand torii repainted in Okayama, restored to its solemn reddish-copper color|newspaper=Sanyō Shimbun|date=2014-09-24|url=http://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1|accessdate=2014-09-28}} * [[:en:1985|Year 1985]] (Shōwa 60): The grand torii was repainted. * [[:en:2009|Year 2009]] (Heisei 21): On April 1, Okayama City became a designated city by government ordinance. With this, the temple’s address changed from “Okayama City Takamatsu Inari” to “Okayama-shi Kita-ku Takamatsu Inari.” * [[:en:2013|Year 2013]] (Heisei 25): On December 3, renovation work on the old Niō Gate was completed, and a commemorative ceremony was held. * [[:en:2014|Year 2014]] (Heisei 26): ** On April 12, a celebration marking the Completionhttp://www.sanyonews.jp/article/72820/1/?rct=okayama1 ** This year, the grand torii was repainted again at a total cost of about 7 million yen. {{ill|Bengala|ja|弁柄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bengara|qq=}} (red ocher) from {{ill|Nishie Residence|ja|西江邸|lt=Nishie-tei|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishie Residence|1=Nishie Residence|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11628966}} was used for the plaque. == Cultural Properties == === Okayama City Designated Important Cultural Property === * Reiō-den Main Hall === National Registered Tangible Cultural Properties ===
